title: Al-Ghafur, the All-Forgiving
tomorrow: a man, a thirsty dog, a shoe full of water. who says thank you?

lines: ONE BY ONE, UNDER A COVER.
cards: Screenshots. Somewhere, on someone's phone, is a picture of the worst thing you ever typed. Receipts, people call them, kept just in case.
So yesterday's question carries weight: on the last day, what does God do with what you hid? A hadith in al-Bukhari answers it as a scene.
Allah draws a believer close, places His cover over him, and goes through his sins one by one. Do you remember this one? And this?
Until the man is sure he's finished. Then Allah says: I covered them for you in the world, and I forgive them for you today.

teach.b: That's Al-Ghafur, the All-Forgiving, who covers faults.
The Qur'an says it to people who've gone too far, in Pickthall's words: "Despair not of the mercy of Allah, Who forgiveth all sins. Lo! He is the Forgiving, the Merciful."
Here's the detail to tell a friend tonight: in that hadith, the forgiving happens under a cover, privately, before anyone else could see.
And a second hadith turns it toward us: whoever covers a Muslim, Allah will cover him. So should you always keep quiet about someone's fault? Two views, both inside the tradition.
The first: cover it. Protect people's dignity, leave room to change, don't be the one passing around the screenshot.
Its best case: exposure rarely helps a person turn around, and the hadith promises a cover for the one who gives one.

teach.h: VIEW TWO: NOT THE ONGOING HARM.
teach.b: The second: cover the slip, not the harm. Commentators on that hadith say covering fits a fault that's over, by someone not known for doing harm, and that a wrong hurting others should reach whoever can stop it.
Its best case: silence can protect the one doing harm while the one being hurt waits. Both care about the same thing. They draw the line in different places, so each case gets weighed.

how: Muslims ask Allah's forgiveness (istighfar) daily and are taught to cover others' private faults (sitr) rather than expose them, while scholars hold that harm to others must be stopped.

o: the one who forgives only small mistakes
the one who forgets every fault at once

games.q: the cover and the forgiving — tap the pairs.

s: "Despair not of the mercy of Allah, Who forgiveth all sins."
in a hadith, the forgiving on the last day happens under a cover
Allah places His cover over the believer: I covered them for you in the world.
covering faults means staying quiet even while someone is being hurt
commentators say covering fits a fault that's over; ongoing harm should reach someone who can stop it.

games.q: your friend keeps quiet about a classmate who's been taking money from the team fund. she says, 'Allah covers faults, so i do too.' what's the best case for the other view?
o: covering faults is never allowed, so she's simply wrong.
cover a slip that's over; harm that's still happening should reach someone who can stop it.
only cover for friends; anyone else's faults are fair game.
games.why: both views value covering. the second draws the line at ongoing harm, because silence can protect the one doing it while others keep paying.

practice: Bring to mind a fault you know about someone, one that's finished and hurts nobody now. Lay one hand over the other in your lap, like a cloth folded over something.
For the sit, let that fault stay under your hand, kept and not passed on.

wordCard.voice: Al-Ghafur. The All-Forgiving, who covers faults first and forgives them under that cover.

orig.note: Arabic: the All-Forgiving. in the hadith, Allah covers the faults, then forgives them.

carryVoice: Your line: he covers, so cover the slip, and never the harm still happening. Until tomorrow, then.

sources.q: Despair not of the mercy of Allah, Who forgiveth all sins. Lo! He is the Forgiving, the Merciful.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 2441 (the najwa: I covered them for you in the world, and I forgive them for you today)
Sahih Muslim 2580, 2699 (whoever covers a Muslim, Allah will cover him)
an-Nawawi, Sharh Sahih Muslim, on 2580 (limits of covering: one not known for harm; ongoing wrongs to be reported)
